claims.case_section: 3. Naval Pejoration and the 1877–1889 Ballahoo Slang Bridge
claims.short_label: 1847–1889 naval pejoration ('ballyhoo of blazes') and metaphorical 'catching ballyhoo' / 'knocked to Ballyhoo'
claims.statement: Between 1847 and 1889, Anglo-American nautical and colloquial print reduced unstressed medial /ə/ to <y> ('ballyhoo') and extended disdain for lubberly schooners into Herman Melville's 'ballyhoo of blazes' (1847 Omoo) and American colloquial idioms of severe reprimand ('catching ballyhoo', May 7, 1889, 29 calendar years before OED's 1918 note) and violent ruin ('knocked to Ballyhoo', May 13, 1889, 16 calendar years before OED's 1905 note).
claims.rationale: Royal Navy writers already ridiculed unhandy 'ballahou' craft in 1826 (CERT-1800-015); Melville's 1847 Omoo (CERT-1800-016) fixed the medial-<y> 'ballyhoo of blazes' contempt epithet for an unseaworthy ship, and 1889 Georgia and Chicago newspaper witnesses show 'ballyhoo' functioning alone in 'blazes/hell' euphemism frames decades ahead of OED's twentieth-century notes.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Medial-<y> spelling 'ballyhoo' and pejorative/euphemistic semantic extension ('dilapidated ship' -> 'blazes, reprimand, ruin') between 1847 and 1889.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Direct semantic equivalence with a carnival sideshow platform without further terrestrial bridge evidence.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: How widely inland speakers using 'knocked to Ballyhoo' in 1889 retained any conscious maritime association with 'ballyhoo of blazes'.

limitations: Idioms like 'knocked to Ballyhoo' may also reflect secondary attraction to Anglo-Irish 'Bally-' place-name euphemisms (cf. CLM-1800-014).

evidence.reason: Herman Melville's 1847 Omoo attesting medial-<y> 'ballyhoo of blazes' for a slovenly, dilapidated vessel.

evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether all five 1877–1884 tokens represent a single semantic development or overlapping colloquial idioms.

claims.statement: Primary print witnesses from 1810 to 1899 document bidirectional orthographic sharing between the nautical vessel noun ('ballahou' 1810, 'balahoo' 1815, 'ballahoo' 1846, 'ballyhoo' 1847) and terrestrial American colloquial and midway usages ('ballyhoo' 1877/1880/1893, 'ballahoo' 1879/1884/1899).
claims.rationale: Before DRAgNEt's 1879, 1884, and 1899 newsprint discoveries, lexicographers split OED's 'ballahoo, n.' / 'ballyhoo, n.1' (maritime) from 'ballyhoo, n.2' (slang/midway) partly on orthographic grounds. Documenting that maritime English adopted <ballyhoo> by 1847 while terrestrial and midway American English retained <ballahoo> in 1879, 1884, and 1899 establishes formal orthographic overlap independent of any etymological hypothesis.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Bidirectional co-occurrence of <ballahoo> and <ballyhoo> across both maritime and non-nautical/midway print traditions.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Unbroken monogenetic semantic transmission from schooners to sideshows (evaluated separately in CLM-1800-013).
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: The relative weight of inherited orthographic memory versus independent schwa-spelling variation (/ˈbæləhuː/).

limitations: Orthographic identity is a necessary compatibility condition rather than sufficient proof of semantic continuity.

claims.target_lexeme: ballahoo, n. (< French Antillean balaou < Island Carib Bálaoû)
claims.short_label: Nautical 'ballahoo' derives from Island Carib 'Bálaoû' (1665) via French Antillean 'balaou' and Eastern Caribbean Spanish 'balahú'
claims.statement: Nautical English 'ballahou' / 'ballahoo' derives from French Antillean 'balaou' ('halfbeak pelagic fish', Labat 1722; extended metaphorically to sleek Martinique/Guadeloupe schooners, Académie 1798 / Jal 1848) and ultimately Island Carib 'Bálaoû' (Breton 1665), with intervocalic '-h-' resolving vocalic hiatus alongside Eastern Caribbean Spanish 'balahú' (Puerto Rico 1831; absent in Pichardo's 1836 Cuban lexicon).
claims.rationale: Primary seventeenth- to nineteenth-century Caribbean dictionaries trace the exact semantic transfer ('slender darting halfbeak fish' -> 'fast-sailing Lesser Antillean schooner') and geographic distribution (Windward/Leeward Islands and Puerto Rico, contrasting with western Cuban 'bajonao'), explaining how British and American mariners borrowed 'ballahou' in West Indian ports by 1777–1810.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Lesser Antillean Carib ('Bálaoû') -> French Creole/colonial French ('balaou') maritime etymology of English nautical 'ballahoo, n.'
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: That American carnival 'ballyhoo' borrowed directly from Carib or French without passing through nineteenth-century English slang.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether English sailors inserted orthographic '-h-' independently at the /a.u/ hiatus or reinforced it via bilingual contact with Puerto Rican/Trinidadian Spanish 'balahú'.

limitations: Applies strictly to the maritime vessel noun (ballahoo, n. / ballyhoo, n.1); downstream extension to midway ballyhoo, n.2 is graded separately in CLM-1800-013.

evidence.reason: Raymond Breton's 1665 Dictionnaire caraïbe-françois recording Island Carib 'Bálaoû' ('small pelagic fish').
Jean-Baptiste Labat's 1722 Nouveau voyage aux isles de l'Amérique documenting French Antillean 'Balaou'.

Augustin Jal's 1848 Glossaire nautique (p. 219) explicitly connecting the Antillean fish 'BALAOU' to the Martinique/Guadeloupe schooner.
Esteban Pichardo's 1836 Cuban dictionary negative control ('BAJONAO', lacking 'balahú'), localizing the maritime term to the Eastern Caribbean / Lesser Antilles.
Accounts for the 1810 Anglo-Caribbean 'ballahou built schooner' borrowing.

claims.case_section: 3. Naval Pejoration and the 1877–1889 Ballahoo Slang Bridge
claims.short_label: Partially supported hypothesis that maritime 'ballahoo'/'ballyhoo' contributed to colloquial and midway 'ballyhoo'
claims.statement: Shared <ballahoo> orthography in 1879–1884 terrestrial American slang and 1899 midway 'ballahoo stage', combined with naval pejoration ('ballyhoo of blazes' -> 'disorderly commotion / noisy political display'), partially supports Atcheson L. Hench's hypothesis that nautical 'ballahoo'/'ballyhoo' contributed to colloquial and midway 'ballyhoo', while the specific institutional transfer into 1893 dime-museum/sideshow platform jargon remains unclosed by any explicit transitional gloss.
claims.rationale: Separating documented orthographic and chronological facts (CLM-1800-004, CLM-1800-005, CLM-1800-011) from the transmission inference keeps the epistemic boundary clear: the 1879–1884 'general ballahoo' / 'whooping-up ballahoo' citations supply the terrestrial phonetic and orthographic bridge Hench (1945, 1965) hypothesized, yet no pre-1893 showman text explicitly explains why a freak-show outside platform pitch was called a 'ballyhoo', leaving room for secondary blending on the variety stage.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Chronological continuity, <ballahoo> orthographic persistence, and pejorative semantic narrowing ('slovenly ship' -> 'blazes/ruin' -> 'noisy political/convention commotion') preceding 1893 midway usage.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: A direct, metalinguistically attested link between maritime or political 'ballahoo/ballyhoo' and International Amusement Company's 1893 Chicago World's Fair 'Ballyhoo Freaks' advertisement.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: How 1880s–1890s dime-museum managers narrowed 'noisy commotion / bombastic display' specifically to the free outside crowd-gathering show.

limitations: Lacks an explicit 1880–1893 dime-museum, circus, or waterfront bridge quotation equating an outside sideshow lecture or platform with naval or political 'ballahoo'/'ballyhoo'.
resolution_criteria: Locate an 1880–1893 dime-museum, street-fair, or circus text explicitly explaining 'ballyhoo'/'ballahoo' or bridging 'whooping-up ballahoo' ('noisy public display') to an outside freak-show platform.
Uncover showman correspondence or trade glossaries from Chicago or New York (1885–1895) documenting pre-Exposition dime-museum adoption.

claims.case_section: 5. Evaluating Competing Origins and Rejected Archival Leads
claims.short_label: Anglo-Irish 'Ballyhooly' and Martin's 1886 Gaiety song are chronologically excluded as primary origin, though plausible secondary convergers
claims.statement: Chronological comparison excludes County Cork 'Ballyhooly' and Robert J. Martin's December 1886 London Gaiety song 'Ballyhooly' as the primary etymon of either 1810 nautical 'ballahou' (76 years earlier) or 1877–1884 American colloquial 'ballyhoo'/'ballahoo' (2 to 9 years before Martin's song), while supporting plausible secondary convergence in idioms ('give \'em Ballyhooly', May 26, 1880) and late-1880s variety-stage familiarity.
claims.rationale: Stephen Goranson and Farmer & Henley (1901) highlighted Irish 'Ballyhooly' ('faction-fighting village; noisy temperance band; tongue-lashing'). Primary scans confirm 'give \'em Ballyhooly' in New York's Puck in May 1880 and American Clipper reprints of Martin's 'Ballyhooley' song in 1887–1888, but neither explains final /-li/ apocope nor accounts for pre-existing 1810–1884 <ballahoo>/<ballyhoo> forms.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Chronological impossibility of Robert J. Martin's 1886 song 'Ballyhooly' originating 1810 nautical 'ballahou' or 1877–1884 American 'ballyhoo'/'ballahoo'.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absence of secondary folk-etymological reinforcement between 'Ballyhooly' and 'ballyhoo' among 1880s–1890s Irish-American variety performers.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Extent of spoken blending between 'give \'em Ballyhooly' (1880) and 'catching ballyhoo' / 'knocked to Ballyhoo' (1889).

limitations: Treats 'Ballyhooly' respectfully as a plausible secondary stage/idiom converger rather than a falsified folk myth.

claims.target_lexeme: ballyhoo (< alleged 1893 Midway Arabic bi-llāhi / 'B'Allah hoo')
claims.case_section: 5. Evaluating Competing Origins and Rejected Archival Leads
claims.short_label: 15-volume (5.91M-character) 1893–1894 Midway Plaisance negative sweep refutes the Arabic 'B\'Allah hoo' origin legend
claims.statement: A full-text sweep across 15 contemporaneous 1893–1894 World's Columbian Exposition Midway Plaisance guidebooks, photofolios, dialect novels, and souvenir histories (5,914,177 OCR characters; 5,879,738 characters in the 14-volume Street in Cairo core plus Holley 1894) returns zero occurrences of 'ballyhoo', 'ballahoo', 'billahi', or 'Allah hoo', recording instead pidgin English cries ('Alla gooda bum-bum!', 'Hot-hot-hot!', 'baksheesh') while English 'Ballyhoo Freaks' was already in print on July 1, 1893—contradicting the 1912 Oriental-origin assertion and the 1935–1936 Wolverton/Mencken 'B\'Allah hoo' anecdote.
claims.rationale: H. L. Mencken (1936) popularized Charles Wolverton and W. O. Taylor's December 1935 recollection (reprinted Jan. 25, 1936 in Editor & Publisher, CERT-1800-215) claiming 1893 Chicago Oriental theater barkers shouted 'B\'Allah hoo'. Auditing nearly six million characters of actual 1893–1894 Midway eyewitness descriptions finds zero such cries, whereas 'ballyhoo'/'ballahoo' existed in American English in 1877–1889 and in Chicago dime-museum trade ads on July 1, 1893.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Zero tokens of 'ballyhoo', 'ballahoo', 'billahi', or 'Allah hoo' across 5,914,177 characters of contemporaneous 1893–1894 Midway Plaisance publications, refuting documentary support for the 1935–1936 Arabic origin story.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Verbatim phonetic transcripts of every unrecorded Arabic utterance on the 1893 Midway, though pre-1893 English 'ballyhoo' independently falsifies 1893 Arabic coinage.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None regarding the retrospective post-hoc status of the 1912 and 1935–1936 Oriental/Arabic anecdotes.

limitations: CERT-1800-215 (January 25, 1936 Editor & Publisher) is post-1930 and verified without a hosted scan.

claims.short_label: Masthead and trade-press audits (65.74M chars) quarantine 8 misdates, OCR ghosts, racehorse 'Ballyhoo', and 'Mt. Ballyhoo'
claims.statement: Primary-scan verification across pre-1915 newsprint and 65.74 million characters of amusement-trade periodicals (1880–1915) quarantines eight non-qualifying leads: three serial metadata misdates ('1880' Dramatic Mirror -> Jan. 8, 1916; '1890' Review of Reviews -> 1932; '1890' Architectural Record -> Mar. 1936), two OCR ghosts ('1856' 'hullabaloo' misread as 'ballahoo'; '1861' 'ballyhov' corruption), two thoroughbred racehorse Ballyhoo turf items (1889–1891, accounting for >150 pre-1893 Clipper hits), and the Unalaska toponym Mt. Ballyhoo (1927, named by Jack London in 1897 after naval 'ballyhoo').
claims.rationale: Auditing every pre-1893 amusement-trade token in The New York Clipper and Google Books serial runs ensures that thoroughbred turf reports, serial-start-year catalog bugs, and OCR corruptions of 'hullabaloo' are cleanly excluded from lexical timelines.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Non-qualifying status of all eight quarantined misdates, OCR corruptions, racehorse names, and toponyms in ballyhoo.json.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Exhaustive absence of pre-1893 show-trade tokens in unindexed local handbills.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None for the eight audited records.

limitations: Post-1930 misdated serial volumes (1932 Review of Reviews CERT-1800-216; March 1936 Architectural Record CERT-1800-217) are verified without hosted WebP scans.
